scenarios.name: New menu feedback
scenarios.goal: We changed our menu. I want input on the new dishes, the choices available, and the prices. Find out what customers like and what we should improve.

questions.text: Since the new menu launched last month, have you eaten at our restaurant and ordered from that menu?
Which of the new dishes did you try?
What did you like or not like about the new dishes you tried?
How satisfied were you with the range of choices on the new menu, on a scale from 1 to 5?
What do you think about the vegetarian choices on the menu now?
How did the portion sizes feel to you?
How did the prices feel for what you received?
Is there anything else you would like to add, or any dishes from the old menu that you miss?

issues: Q2 asks which new dishes they tried, but some respondents may have ordered from the new menu without trying one of the six new mains; they may have tried revised existing dishes or only noticed prices/choice changes.
Q4's 1-to-5 satisfaction scale would be clearer on the phone if the endpoints are read aloud, for example '1 means very dissatisfied and 5 means very satisfied.'
Q5 is relevant, but for non-vegetarian customers it may produce weak answers unless it allows 'I did not look at vegetarian choices' or probes whether vegetarian choice matters to their group.
Q7 is broad and good, but if price sensitivity is a key issue after a 10% increase, it may help to include a follow-up or scale about value for money.
improvements: Revise Q2 to: 'Which dishes did you order from the new menu, including any new dishes, if you remember?'
Revise Q4 to: 'How satisfied were you with the range of choices on the new menu, where 1 means very dissatisfied and 5 means very satisfied?'
Revise Q5 to: 'Did you notice the vegetarian choices on the menu? If yes, what did you think about them?'
Consider adding: 'Compared with your previous visits, did the menu prices feel lower, about the same, a little higher, or much higher?'
Consider adding a short prioritization question: 'If we changed one thing about the new menu, what should it be?'

report.headline: The new menu has real uptake and several dishes have clear appeal, especially dal makhani, paneer tikka pasta, and mutton rogan josh. The main improvement areas are value for the higher prices, smaller or uneven portions, reduced vegetarian variety, and consistency in sauces, spice, and what is included.

themes.title: Customers are engaging with the new menu and key dishes are getting tried
themes.description: Many respondents said they had ordered from the new menu, including some repeat visits. The dishes most often discussed across answers were paneer tikka pasta, dal makhani, mutton rogan josh, and the vegetarian thali, giving useful feedback on the main menu changes.

themes.title: Dal makhani is one of the strongest new-menu items, but consistency matters
themes.description: Many people described dal makhani positively as smooth, rich, creamy, comforting, or flavorful. A smaller but important set of comments said it was less thick than before, too salty, had more tomato tang, or needed more gravy, so the dish appears liked but sensitive to execution.

themes.title: Paneer tikka pasta has standout flavor but repeated portion and sauce issues
themes.description: Customers often liked the pasta’s smoky, creamy, or tasty flavor, but the same dish drew recurring complaints about small paneer pieces, less paneer than before, oily or heavy sauce, dryness, saltiness, blandness, or inconsistent texture. This dish is visible enough that fixing it could improve both satisfaction and perceived value.

themes.title: Rogan josh earns praise for flavor, but meat quantity and value are weak spots
themes.description: Several people liked the rogan josh for rich or deep flavor, aroma, spice, tenderness, or how the masala worked with rice. Concerns centered on fewer or smaller mutton pieces, portion size, occasional toughness or oily gravy, and whether the dish justifies the higher price.

themes.title: Vegetarian variety feels reduced, especially for families and groups
themes.description: Many respondents said vegetarian choices feel fewer than before, especially mains, gravies, or thali options. Some still felt the remaining vegetarian dishes are good, but several said the reduced range makes group or family ordering harder and mentioned missing older vegetarian items.

themes.title: Price concerns are mostly about portions and included value, not price alone
themes.description: Many customers said prices felt high, expensive, or not worth it, and they often linked this to smaller portions, less meat or paneer, thinner gravy, or weaker sides. Others said the higher prices were acceptable when taste stayed strong and portions or inclusions matched expectations.

themes.title: Thali, sides, and menu clarity need tighter expectations
themes.description: Thali feedback repeatedly mentioned uneven sides, basic accompaniments, repetitive flavors, unbalanced items, bland items, less filling gravies, or not enough bread and sides. Separately, some people said vegetarian labels, what is included, or add-on pricing was unclear.

requests: Increase paneer quantity or paneer piece size in paneer tikka pasta and other paneer dishes.

Improve consistency in spice, sauce, and gravy thickness, including an option for stronger or milder spice.
Adjust paneer tikka pasta sauce so it is less oily or heavy and more consistently creamy and flavorful.

nextSteps.suggestion: Prioritize a paneer tikka pasta fix: increase visible paneer, reduce heaviness or oiliness, and standardize creaminess, salt, and sauce flavor.
Restore vegetarian breadth in a targeted way, such as adding one rotating paneer or veg gravy and testing the return of an old vegetarian starter or old-style veg thali element.
Redesign the thali specification so sides, gravies, bread, salad, and achar feel balanced rather than basic, repetitive, or uneven.
Update the menu layout to state vegetarian labels, what comes with each dish, portion expectations where useful, and which add-ons cost extra.
Offer clearer spice-level choices or guidance for dishes with variable heat, including milder family-friendly options and a stronger rogan josh option for customers who want it.

issues: The first theme understates uptake by labeling it as 10 people even though the raw screening question shows almost everyone said they had eaten and ordered from the new menu; if the count is only for quoted/theme-coded mentions, the description should avoid implying total uptake count.

The uptake theme uses only generic "Yes" quotes, which do not substantiate the specific claim that paneer tikka pasta, dal makhani, rogan josh, and veg thali were the most discussed dishes. Those claims are supported by the raw answers, but not by the displayed quotes.
Price/value is well covered, but the next steps do not directly say to review price architecture or add value through portion/side changes despite this being one of the strongest patterns.

Overall choice satisfaction ratings are not summarized numerically or qualitatively beyond vegetarian variety. The raw scores suggest moderate-to-good satisfaction with range, with a minority of low scores, which would help balance the reduced-veg-variety finding.

Portion size is mostly handled through price/value and disagreements rather than a full theme, even though small or uneven portions recur across pasta, rogan josh, thali, and dal makhani/gravy comments.

The report says people counts are code-computed, but some disagreement counts for price/value look low relative to the many raw price comments describing prices as high, slightly high, expensive, steep, or not worth it. This may be due to narrower coding categories, but it could confuse a reader.
missed_patterns: Several respondents specifically referenced about a 10% price increase; the report mentions higher prices generally but does not highlight the repeated 10% anchor as a customer expectation-setting issue.

Old-menu nostalgia clusters around vegetarian starters/manchurian-style items, chana masala, old veg thali format, and old dal makhani; the report mentions old vegetarian items but could be more specific about which ones to test bringing back.

Some non-veg/chicken feedback appears in the raw answers, including inconsistent chicken heat and chicken biryani-style rice being less rich, but the report appropriately prioritizes larger patterns and only indirectly covers spice consistency.

Family/group ordering appears repeatedly in vegetarian variety, thali, spice-for-kids, and portion comments; the report mentions families/groups in the veg theme but could make family/group usability a clearer product-design lens.
strengths: The headline is accurate and captures the main story: strong dish appeal alongside value, portion, vegetarian variety, and consistency concerns.

Theme descriptions are generally faithful to the raw answers and supported by verbatim quotes, especially for dal makhani, paneer tikka pasta, rogan josh, vegetarian variety, price/value, and thali issues.

The report distinguishes nuanced positives from negatives: dal makhani is liked but consistency-sensitive; paneer tikka pasta stands out but needs execution fixes; rogan josh has flavor appeal but meat/value concerns.
Gaps are stated plainly by question, and the report discloses that there were 54 responses with 3 text simulations.

Next steps are mostly actionable and follow from the evidence: improve paneer quantity/sauce consistency, restore targeted vegetarian breadth, redesign thali components, clarify inclusions/add-ons, and offer spice-level guidance.

asks.question: Which dishes got the most criticism and why?
asks.answer: Paneer tikka pasta appears to be the most criticized dish: repeated complaints were small/too little paneer, small serving for the price, and sauce or seasoning problems such as oily, heavy, too creamy, bland, salty, dry, or inconsistent (e109, e112, e115, e121, e123, e127, e128, e134, e136, e137, e140, e142, e144, e145, e147, e148, e150, e156, e157, e160, e161, e162). Vegetarian thali/veg mains were another major criticism area: respondents said thali items or sides were smaller, uneven, basic, repetitive, bland, or less filling, and several said vegetarian options feel fewer now (e113, e117, e119, e135, e136, e141, e146, e154, e160, e217, e221, e227, e236, e237, e241, e243, e245, e265, e267, e269). Mutton rogan josh also drew recurring criticism for too little or smaller mutton, small portions, oily/thin/inconsistent gravy, tough meat, long wait, or mild spice (e116, e118, e125, e130, e132, e138, e143, e148, e151, e158). Dal makhani was often praised, but the criticisms were that it was less thick or had too little gravy, stronger/tangier or less buttery than before, too salty, too small, or not as missed/liked as the old version (e109, e115, e118, e125, e128, e133, e134, e140, e150, e155, e161, e425).

asks.question: Are the price complaints about the price itself or the portion size?
asks.answer: The complaints are both, but many customers framed the issue as value for money: prices felt high because portions, meat/paneer quantity, thali sides, or overall fullness did not match the increase. Examples include “expensive for the portion size,” “portion was smaller,” “meat quantity didn’t” rise with the ~10% price increase, “prices high for quantity,” and “prices higher and portions feel smaller.” There were also some complaints about the price itself or quality-for-price—such as “not worth it at this price,” “too expensive for the quality,” and “too high”—so lowering prices may help some, but the stronger actionable theme is to improve portion/quantity/sides and consistency to make the higher prices feel justified.

scenarios.name: Society event feedback
scenarios.goal: Call attendees of our evening talk and hands-on lighting session and find out what worked and what we should improve for the next event.

Overall, how useful was the event for you, on a scale from 1 to 5, where 1 is not useful and 5 is very useful?

issues: Q4 is broad and may not prompt specifics about the three-station format, waiting time, ability to try equipment, or instruction quality.
Q5 appropriately addresses a known concern, but because it names crowding it may slightly foreground that issue; still phrased neutrally enough.
For respondents who attended only the talk or only the hands-on session, later questions about the missed component need interviewer skip logic to avoid awkward answers.
improvements: Add skip instructions: ask Q3 only if attended the talk; ask Q4 only if attended the hands-on session; if Q1 is 'I did not attend,' ask why they could not attend or end the survey.
Consider splitting Q4 into a more concrete phone-friendly prompt: 'What worked well or badly at the lighting stations—for example, getting a turn, understanding what to do, or the equipment setup?'
Add a quick rating or probe on event logistics if desired: 'How was the timing, room, and organization of the evening?'
If prioritizing improvements, follow Q6 with: 'Why would that change make the biggest difference?'

report.headline: Overall, attendees found the evening useful because the photographer made lighting practical and the stations let them see changes directly. The main improvement area is operational: crowding, sound, and station flow often limited how much people could hear, see, and practise.

themes.title: The talk made lighting feel practical and repeatable
themes.description: Attendees repeatedly praised real wedding examples, venue-based case studies, step-by-step lighting decisions, diagrams, before-and-after comparisons, and concrete Q&A. These elements helped people understand ratios, modifiers, flash-and-ambient balance, posing, backgrounds, and how to troubleshoot a setup.

quotes.value: His wedding examples made the lighting logic click.
He explained lighting like a story, and the wedding context helped.
The breakdown of exposure and lighting ratios was clear, and he fixed one problem step by step.

themes.title: Hands-on practice worked when attendees could access it
themes.description: People valued being able to adjust lights, try modifiers, compare soft and hard light, and see results quickly. Instructor or assistant corrections were especially helpful because they made changes in angle, shadows, sync, or light direction immediately visible.

quotes.value: Good concept and I learned how to place lights. The time felt short and the demos were quick, so we didn’t get enough chances to repeat.
Stations were excellent once I got in; the instructor corrected my modifier angle and I could see the difference right away.
Really helpful. I was able to adjust the key light and see the effect right away.

themes.title: Crowding reduced practice time, movement, visibility, and comfort
themes.description: The most consistent barrier was that the station area felt packed, causing queues, short turns, blocked views, difficulty reaching stations, and less chance to repeat or experiment. Several also said tight space made moving lights, tripods, stands, or testing angles uncomfortable or less safe.

quotes.value: Great hands-on, but crowded—I had to wait to touch the modifiers.

themes.title: Room sound and mic issues made instructions hard to follow
themes.description: Across both the talk and stations, attendees described echo, overlapping conversations, music, flash noise, outside sound, and inconsistent microphones. This often made small instructions, station guidance, announcements, or talk audio harder to hear.

quotes.value: Hands-on but a scramble—people waited, and the room sound made it distracting.

themes.title: Station flow and instructions need more structure
themes.description: People said rotations, demos, and instructions sometimes felt rushed or confusing, especially when arriving at a busy station. Requests clustered around assigned times, clearer queues, posted or printed station steps, countdowns, signs, floor tape, and repeated instructions.

quotes.value: Good concept and I learned how to place lights. The time felt short and the demos were quick, so we didn’t get enough chances to repeat.

themes.title: Attendees want more guided practice, not just quick exposure
themes.description: Beyond reducing crowding, several asked for longer station rounds, clearer time windows, more studio time, fewer setups with deeper guidance, or photographers staying longer for one-on-one help. The reason was that people wanted time to repeat, vary, and understand each setup.

quotes.value: Good concept and I learned how to place lights. The time felt short and the demos were quick, so we didn’t get enough chances to repeat.

themes.title: Follow-up learning would extend the value of the event
themes.description: Several attendees asked for an editing or review component to apply the lighting look, while others wanted outdoor or outdoor-like practice to compare lighting conditions. People also asked for take-home materials such as settings checklists, cheat sheets, recommended settings, or recorded slides and diagrams.

These comments point to pacing, diagram size, screen visibility, and catch-up materials as secondary improvements.

nextSteps.suggestion: Plan the next hands-on portion for smaller groups: cap attendance, use a larger room, split into waves, or run back-to-back station sessions.
Build a formal station rotation plan with assigned time windows, clear queues, countdowns, signs or floor tape, and enough spacing between stations.
Increase practice depth by lengthening station rounds, starting stations on time, using fewer setups with more guided practice, or keeping photographers at stations longer for one-on-one help.
Treat audio as part of the event setup: run a mic and announcements check, consider headset or external mics, reduce music, and separate briefing or talk areas from shooting stations where possible.
Prepare station reference materials: printed quick guides or cheat sheets with setup steps, suggested camera settings, and reminders, then send recommended settings or key diagrams afterward.
Add a short editing or review follow-up so attendees can work with the images they shot and connect lighting choices to finished results.
Consider an outdoor walk or outdoor-like lighting station to help attendees compare natural light with the studio lighting techniques.
For the talk, keep the practical case-study style but add safeguards for accessibility: larger diagrams or screen, slightly slower pacing, and Q&A pauses or catch-up materials.

issues: The report is generally faithful and actionable. The main honesty caveat is that representativeness is only implicit: it lists participation figures and says there were 56 responses with 3 text simulations, but it does not plainly explain what the 3 simulations mean or how much weight to place on findings from a partly simulated/phone-reached sample.

Participation/completion figures are potentially confusing next to the raw survey base: the report says 80 people, 74 reached, 53 completed, and 56 responses. This may be internally explainable because of simulations, but the report should clarify it for an organizer.

The report does not explicitly note that one respondent said they did not attend, and several talk/station questions include people who skipped or did not attend that portion. This is minor because the themes still reflect the answered data, but it affects interpretation.

A few themes overlap substantially: crowding, station flow, and desire for more guided practice are distinct but interrelated. The report handles this reasonably, though an organizer might benefit from seeing them prioritized as one operational package.
missed_patterns: A small operational point appears only weakly in the report: start stations on time / communicate the schedule earlier. This was mentioned by a few respondents and is partly covered under clearer scheduling, but not called out directly.

Requests for one guide per station or more photographer/assistant presence are present in next steps but could be emphasized slightly more because guidance corrections were a major reason the hands-on session worked well.

Talk praise included some specific content areas—lighting for different skin tones, posing/background cleanliness, wedding workflow and communicating with couples—that are summarized broadly but not surfaced as distinct strengths.
strengths: The headline accurately captures both the main positive finding—practical lighting instruction and direct hands-on learning—and the main improvement area—crowding, sound, and flow.
Theme descriptions are well supported by verbatim quotes and do not overstate beyond the evidence.

The report covers the major patterns across the raw answers: strong usefulness, effective practical talk, valuable hands-on corrections, crowding/queues, audio problems, rushed/confusing station flow, desire for longer practice, and follow-up learning materials or editing/outdoor sessions.

Next steps are concrete and directly traceable to attendee suggestions, including smaller groups, rotations, audio setup, reference materials, editing follow-up, and accessibility improvements for the talk.
The gaps section provides skipped/not-asked information for each question, and the report acknowledges simulated responses, even if that caveat could be clearer.

asks.question: Was the hands-on session a success or a problem?
asks.answer: The hands-on session looks like a qualified success: people who got access often found it useful, citing immediate feedback, visible lighting changes, trying multiple setups, and confidence-building practice. But it was also a significant operational problem because crowding, queues, rushed rotations, noise/audio issues, and limited space kept several attendees from practicing fully or even reaching stations. The clearest next-step is to keep the hands-on format but run it with more space, smaller or staggered groups, clearer rotations, and better audio/instructions.

asks.question: What should the next event be, based on what members asked for?
asks.answer: Based on member requests, the next event should be a smaller-group, longer hands-on lighting workshop in a larger/quieter space: members asked for “more space,” “smaller batches,” fewer people per station, assigned or timed rotations, and longer practice time [e281, e284, e288, e295, e306, e315, e316]. It should also include clearer station structure—posted/printed guides, a rotation route, and repeated instructions—because members asked for clearer station instructions, quick guides, floor-tape/signage routes, and cheat sheets [e303, e311, e313, e321, e379]. Add a short editing follow-up and/or settings sheet, plus an optional outdoor natural-light walk, since members requested editing workshops/clinics, recommended settings, and outdoor walk practice [e338, e305, e317, e322, e337, e368]. Finally, improve the audio/mic setup or separate the briefing/talk area, because members specifically requested better acoustics, better audio, headset/external mics, and quieter/separate spaces [e283, e292, e300, e318, e323].

issues: Q1 is a strong screener, but the description "the single page with a sample invoice" may be hard for some respondents to recognize or may over-specify the experience if they do not remember the design details.

Q4 asks only about usefulness of the sample invoice for making an invoice, which is relevant, but it may miss other possible roles the sample invoice played, such as understanding fields, pricing, taxes, or workflow.

Q6 introduces bank account connection without context from the stated goal. It may be important to activation, but if bank connection was not a prominent onboarding task, respondents may wonder why it is being asked.
Q7 combines "create or send" first invoice. Creating and sending are different milestones; a respondent who created one quickly but never sent it may not know which answer to give.
Q7 response options are not fully exhaustive for people who created an invoice but have not sent one, or who cannot remember the timing.
improvements: Revise Q1 slightly for phone clarity: "In the last three weeks, did you sign up for the invoicing app and see the new onboarding page with a sample invoice?"

Consider adding a broad needs question before the closing: "After onboarding, what did you still need in order to feel ready to send your first invoice?" This directly addresses the goal's 'what they still needed to get started.'
Split or clarify Q7: "About how long after signing up did you create your first invoice?" and, if relevant, "Have you sent an invoice yet?"
Add "I do not remember" or "Not sure" to Q7.
If bank account connection is central, introduce Q6 in more natural language: "During onboarding, the app may have asked you to connect a bank account. Which best describes what happened?"
For Q4, phone wording could be smoother: "From 1 to 5, where 1 is not at all useful and 5 is very useful, how useful was the sample invoice for understanding how to make your own?"

report.headline: The new onboarding appears to be working best when people use the sample invoice as a filled-out model: it helps them see the invoice structure, fields, line items, totals, and due dates, and several also liked the simpler one-page flow. The main drag on getting started is bank connection, both because it fails or loops for some users and because many are unsure whether it is required before creating or sending an invoice.

themes.description: People repeatedly said the filled sample invoice made it clear what to enter and where, including client details, invoice numbers, due dates, payment terms, line items, taxes, totals, rates, hours, amounts, and currency. Ratings also generally reflected that it was useful or very useful for understanding how to make an invoice.

nextSteps.suggestion: Make the bank step explicitly deferrable if the product allows it: label what users can do now, what requires bank connection, and offer a clear path such as creating a draft first and connecting the bank later.

Add bank-linking explanation and trust microcopy before authentication: why it is needed, whether it links a business or personal account, what permissions or documents are requested, and which option/account type to choose.
Prioritize debugging and recovery for bank connection failures, including timeout handling, redirect-loop detection, clearer error messages, retry guidance, and an in-flow support route.
Run a mobile usability pass on onboarding and bank connection: enlarge prompts, make next taps obvious, avoid blank-screen moments, and improve mobile invoice preview or tips.

Turn the sample invoice into a small template library with copy/duplicate actions, including recurring monthly, retainer, fixed-price, hourly, consultancy, design, software milestone, and multi-service examples.

Add lightweight invoice-field guidance below or beside the sample: required versus optional labels, field notes, service-description examples, a setup checklist, payment-term definitions, and tax/VAT/discount/currency examples.

issues: The report understates the breadth of the sample-invoice finding: almost every answer to the 'what helped' question mentions the sample invoice, but the theme is labeled '14 people.' Even if code-derived, the description 'strongest onboarding aid' is accurate but the count will read too low relative to the raw answers.

The usefulness-rating disagreement section appears to undercount high ratings: the raw 51 ratings are overwhelmingly 4s and 5s, with only six 3s and one 2. It says 'Many rated 4 or 5 (22),' which is directionally right but visibly too low compared with the listed ratings.

The onboarding completion disagreement count also looks low: there are many more than 37 clear 'Yes' answers among 52 responses. The qualitative conclusion is fine, but the displayed counts do not seem to match the raw list.
Participation metadata says 53 responses with '3 text simulations.' That is a useful caveat, but the report does not explain which responses were simulated or how that affects confidence.

Gaps are stated as skipped/declined/not asked, but the raw prompt only gives answered counts. Some gap labels, such as skipped vs not asked, cannot be independently verified from the raw answers shown.

There is limited synthesis of first-invoice timing. The report uses it indirectly but does not explicitly say that many respondents still took days or had not sent an invoice, which is relevant to the goal of getting started.
missed_patterns: First-invoice timing is mixed: among 35 answers, some created/sent during the same session or later the same day, but many took within a few days, more than a few days, or had not sent one yet. This would help quantify whether onboarding is translating into activation.

A small but repeated need for recurring/monthly billing appears both in improvement suggestions and final comments; the report covers this well in suggestions but could elevate it as a 'still needed to get started' pattern, not just a sample-invoice enhancement.

Several respondents had no blockers or said bank connection worked smoothly / onboarding was straightforward. The report includes disagreement counts but the main themes are understandably problem-focused and do not dwell on this minority.

Trust/account-type concerns around bank linking include business vs personal account, permissions/documents, scary prompts, and generic copy. The report mentions these, but they could be framed as trust/comprehension risk in addition to usability.
strengths: The headline accurately captures the dominant pattern: the sample invoice is working, while bank connection is the main drag on onboarding.
Themes are well supported by verbatim quotes and do not appear to invent unsupported claims.
The report separates bank-link technical failures from bank-link purpose/timing confusion, which is an important and actionable distinction.
Mobile issues are appropriately called out as a cross-cutting problem supported by several raw answers.
Next steps follow directly from the evidence and are concrete enough for product/design/engineering teams to act on.
The report covers the main requested dimensions: what helped, where people got stuck, and what they still needed, including templates, recurring invoices, field guidance, and bank troubleshooting.
Representativeness/gaps are included, including low answer counts for optional improvement and final-comment questions.

asks.question: Where do people get stuck most often?
asks.answer: People got stuck most often at the bank-connection step. Among the 49 people who answered Q3, I count 40 bank-connection-related issues or questions, including verification errors/timeouts/freezes, redirects or loops, unclear whether bank linking was mandatory or what it was for, account-type/permission uncertainty, and mobile readability/blank-screen problems. Other sticking points mentioned were scattered: taxes or payment terms, recurring/monthly invoice setup, template choice, logo/header consistency, and a few people said they had no real blocker.

asks.question: Did the sample invoice help people?
asks.answer: Yes. Among people who answered the 1–5 usefulness question, 44 of 51 rated the sample invoice 4 or 5; open responses also said it helped them see line items and totals, copy due dates/payment terms, understand field order, and know where client details, items, and due dates go. The main caveat is that some respondents still wanted clearer mandatory/optional field notes, more template variations, recurring-invoice examples, and payment-terms/tax/VAT guidance.

issues: Q1 screens for any relevant contact in the past six weeks, but it does not identify which parts of the experience the patient actually had; later questions may be asked of people who did not book, check in, receive follow-up, or have billing questions.
Q2 combines booking and changing an appointment; patients who did both may have different experiences, and patients who only used online/in-person booking may need a clearer prompt.
Q3 response options are slightly unbalanced: 'Short' and 'Too long' are subjective, while 'Acceptable' is evaluative; it may miss 'could not get through' or 'no answer/call back'.
Q4 should include an explicit skip option for patients who did not visit the clinic in person during the period.
Q5 asks only whether reminders had needed information, but not whether reminders arrived on time or through the right channel, which may be important with a new booking system.
Q6 should include an explicit 'I did not have billing questions' skip, otherwise respondents may feel forced to answer a non-applicable open question.
The set asks about follow-up only indirectly through reminders and the final fix question; it may miss post-visit calls, WhatsApp/messages, test reports, treatment plans, or callbacks.
improvements: After Q1, add or use branching: 'Which of these did you do in the past six weeks: booked or changed an appointment, called the clinic, checked in at the clinic, received reminders, had follow-up contact, asked billing questions?'
Revise Q2 to: 'If you booked or changed an appointment, how did it go? What worked well or poorly?'
Revise Q3 options to include: 'I did not call / Got through quickly / Wait was acceptable / Wait was too long / Could not get through or did not get a call back.'
Revise Q4 to: 'If you visited the clinic, how was check-in when you arrived?'
Revise Q5 to cover timing and content: 'If you received an appointment reminder, was it timely and did it include the information you needed?'
Revise Q6 to: 'If you had any billing or payment questions, how were they handled?' and allow 'not applicable'.
Add a follow-up-specific question: 'After your visit or call, did the front desk follow up as expected? Please tell us about any callbacks, messages, or information you were waiting for.'

themes.description: Patients reported reminders that were missing, late, vague, confusing, or wrong about time, date, location, entrance, or updated slot. themes.title: Check-in is often friendly and smooth, but the new system causes repeated details and lookup delays

themes.title: Staff tone is a strength to preserve
themes.description: Even when the process was slow or confusing, patients often described the new staff as polite, professional, friendly, sweet, careful with details, or helpful. This suggests the main fixes are workflow, system, and communication support rather than basic courtesy.

themes.description: Among the patients who discussed billing, several found explanations unclear or incomplete, especially around GST, invoice line items, payment splits, estimate versus final amounts, and receipt details for insurance. nextSteps.suggestion: Create a rescheduling workflow in the booking system that updates the appointment record, confirmation SMS, and reminder together, so patients do not have to rebook from scratch or call repeatedly.
Run a front-desk system refresher focused on finding appointments, verifying updated slots, avoiding duplicate forms, and handling insurance checks before patients arrive.

Build a short billing and insurance script or checklist covering GST breakup, invoice line items, payment split, estimate versus final amount, receipt sharing, and insurance documents, with a clear owner for follow-up.
Preserve and reinforce the team’s friendly patient handling while fixing workflows, because courtesy was often praised even in slower interactions.
Update the outreach list so the patient who asked not to be called again is excluded from future campaign calls.

issues: The check-in theme description includes both positives and system problems, but its supporting quotes are almost entirely positive; it should include quotes about repeated forms, missing records, insurance verification, wrong appointment times, or system search delays to substantiate the problem side.
Next steps do not directly address one of the largest findings: long phone hold times, transfers, call access, and silent waiting. A concrete phone-access fix should be included.

Next steps only indirectly address reminders through rescheduling. The report should add an explicit reminder/confirmation template and QA step for all appointments, covering exact date/time, doctor/department, location/entrance, where to report, what to bring, and changed-slot confirmation.
The report states there were 3 text simulations but does not explain which findings may be affected or how much weight to place on them; representativeness is only lightly handled.

Reminder disagreement undercounts the practical reminder problem if many “Not sure” answers were actually due to unclear, incomplete, or inconsistent reminders; the theme itself captures this better than the disagreement line.
Participation and gap metrics are presented, but some skipped/declined/not-asked details cannot be verified from the raw answers shown and may be confusing to an organizer without explanation.
missed_patterns: Patients specifically disliked silent hold time/hold music, not just the length of phone waits.

Several patients mentioned being pushed from online booking to phone for changes; the report covers this, but the operational implication could be sharper: enable self-service changes or call-back support for changes.

Reminder content issues include wrong entrance/location, where to stand/report, documents to bring, doctor/department name, and vague “confirm/visit soon” language; the report summarizes these but next steps should operationalize them.
There are a few signage/arrival-wayfinding issues at check-in, especially changed signage and unclear registration location.
Insurance verification at check-in appears both as a delay source and as a documentation/checklist need.
strengths: The headline is accurate and specific: it balances friendly staff and smooth check-ins with the main operational failures.
Major patterns in the raw answers are covered: phone waits, fragile rescheduling, reminders, check-in system issues, staff tone, and billing/insurance clarity.
Theme descriptions are generally faithful to the raw answers, and the quoted examples are verbatim.
The report appropriately distinguishes courtesy/staff tone from workflow and system problems, which is useful for management action.
Gaps are explicitly listed, and the report notes that some responses were simulations.

asks.question: Is the new team doing better or worse than the old one on the phone?
asks.answer: I can’t determine whether the new team is doing better or worse than the old one on the phone, because the evidence list only contains recent/new-team phone wait experiences and no comparable old-team phone wait data. The recent evidence does show ongoing phone issues: several respondents said the wait was “Too long,” including waits described as around 12 minutes, more than 15 minutes, almost 20 minutes, about 15 minutes twice, and about 15 minutes on hold. There were also some positive or neutral recent phone reports, with respondents saying waits were “Acceptable” or “Short,” so what’s missing is the old-team baseline to compare against.

asks.question: What single fix would help most patients?
asks.answer: The single fix likely to help the most patients is to fix appointment reminders/confirmation messages: make them reliable, accurate after reschedules, and clear on exact date, time, location/where to report, and what to bring. Among the 30 people who answered the “most important thing to fix” question, 20 mentioned reminders or confirmation-message clarity/accuracy/reliability, often alongside phone wait time; this was the most common fix theme among those who answered.

report.headline: Overall, responses point to a willing volunteer pool for the next three months, with Saturday mornings as the clearest scheduling anchor but continued need for weekday evening options and flexible backups. The biggest operational asks are clearer advance communication, role-specific instructions, and better logistics for driving, reporting points, parking, and accessibility.

nextSteps.suggestion: Build the three-month roster around Saturday mornings as the main anchor, but preserve a weekday evening track and a flexible backup list for people whose work, travel, or classes vary.

Create a shared blackout calendar before assigning shifts, highlighting named conflicts in August, September, October, November, and December, and follow up with volunteers whose conflicts are conditional or not yet finalized.

Set up a WhatsApp-based communication workflow with the roster, venue and parking details, route changes, and a day-before message that includes exact timings, reporting point, task list, and who to contact.
Prepare one-page role packs for packing, front desk, outreach, and driving, including checklists, scripts, what to record or say, handoff sequence, and end-of-shift reporting.

Finalize a driver protocol before assigning driving shifts: reimbursement rules and timing, fuel/parking/toll coverage, required documents, route plan, pickup/drop order, pickup address, and car checklist.

Use role matching rather than open assignment: assign willing drivers only where eligibility and route comfort are clear, avoid outreach for people who named anxiety or discomfort, avoid front desk for people uncomfortable with crowds or phones, and avoid heavy lifting or long packing where people raised physical limits.
Run a brief induction or refresher before shifts, covering safety, hygiene, respectful communication, emergency contacts, and issue reporting, and provide visible IDs or arm bands where possible.
Add practical comfort supports at the site: chairs or seating for front desk, clear check-in signboards, easy access where possible, labeled boxes, and a trolley for cartons.

issues: Participation metadata is confusing and not reconciled with the raw answers: it reports 80 people called/ready and 51 completed while the dataset shown contains 53 responses, and the note '2 text simulations' is not explained.

The availability theme is directionally accurate, but its supporting quotes are all just 'Yes', so they do not substantiate the uncertainty/unavailability part of the description or the cadence claims.

Several theme quote sets are not very representative of the described nuance: the scheduling theme only quotes Saturday mornings despite mentioning weekday evenings/both/varies, and the role-interest theme only quotes packing despite describing broad role interest and limitations.
The report states gaps question-by-question, but does not plainly discuss representativeness of the whole dataset or what the simulated responses mean for confidence.

The frequency question is folded into the availability theme, but the report does not separately summarize the strong pattern that most who answered expect to volunteer monthly to multiple times per month, with a smaller weekly group.
missed_patterns: Packing appears to be the largest first-choice role, with driving also substantial but constrained; this could have been stated more explicitly rather than only saying role interest is broad.
A large share of support requests specifically mention WhatsApp and day-before/advance communication; the report captures this but could quantify or emphasize it as the dominant operational channel.
Blackout conflicts cluster heavily around September/October/November exam, travel, work, and family periods, not just being evenly spread across all months.
Some availability is conditional on weather/health, especially heavy rain and knee/medical issues, which has implications for backup staffing and accessibility.
strengths: The headline accurately captures the main operational story: high willingness, Saturday as the strongest anchor, need for weekday/flexible options, and a strong demand for clearer logistics.
Major themes align well with the raw answers: availability, scheduling, blackout dates, role preferences/limits, driving constraints, communication needs, and practical support are all covered.
Next steps are concrete and well tied to evidence, especially the WhatsApp workflow, driver protocol, role matching, blackout calendar, and role-specific one-page guides.
The report appropriately identifies driving as both a desired role and a constrained assignment area because of reimbursement, routes, licenses, vehicles, traffic, and health concerns.
The gaps section is detailed at the question level and makes clear that later questions had fewer answers than the core availability and timing questions.

asks.question: How many volunteers can cover weekday evenings?
asks.answer: Among the people who answered Q2, 19 volunteers selected either “Weekday evenings” or “Both,” so 19 can be counted as able to cover weekday evenings. Two additional “It varies” responses mention an evening lean (“prefer weekday evenings if I can” and “mostly evenings”), but I have not included them in the firm count because they did not select “Weekday evenings” or “Both.”

asks.question: What support do volunteers ask for most?
asks.answer: Among the 33 people who answered the support question, the most common ask is clearer advance coordination: shift schedules or exact times, checklists, written instructions, role/task briefings, reporting points, and who to contact or report to. The next recurring asks are WhatsApp updates/reminders and driver-specific clarity on reimbursement, routes, pickup/drop points, documents, fuel, parking, or tolls. Smaller but repeated needs include safety/orientation support, role scripts, IDs/vests/arm bands, chairs/easy access, labeled boxes, trolleys, parking details, and pairing for first-timers.
